specPoints.text: understand how an increase in greenhouse gases results in an enhanced greenhouse effect and that this may lead to global warming and its consequences

primer.text: The greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life, but human emissions are turning it up. This note explains the natural trapping of heat by greenhouse gases, then traces the consequences of the enhanced effect: warming oceans, extreme weather, habitat loss and falling biodiversity.

lessons.title: The Natural Greenhouse Machine
lessons.opening: The greenhouse effect is the natural process that keeps Earth liveable: radiation from the sun warms the surface, the surface re-emits heat, and greenhouse gases in the atmosphere trap part of that heat before it escapes to space.
keyPoints: The sun emits radiation that enters the atmosphere of the Earth.
The surface absorbs the energy and re-emits it as heat, in the form of infrared radiation.
Some heat escapes to space, while greenhouse gases absorb and trap the rest in the atmosphere.
This natural trapping is what keeps the planet warm enough for life to survive.

low.restatement: Sunlight warms the ground, the ground breathes out heat, and the gases hold some of it in.
low.analogy: A car parked in the sun with the windows up — warmth gets in and cannot fully leave.
low.examPointer: Name infrared radiation as the re-emitted heat and give carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour as trappers.

medium.restatement: The sequence matters: solar radiation passes in, the surface absorbs it and re-emits infrared, part of that heat escapes to space and part is absorbed by greenhouse gases, and this balance of trapping is what lifts the planet above freezing and keeps it habitable.
medium.analogy: A duvet over a sleeper: body heat passes into the duvet, and only some of it leaks out.
medium.examPointer: Stress that the natural effect is essential — the enhancement by human emissions is the problem.

check.stem: Which type of radiation does the surface of the Earth re-emit after absorbing sunlight?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Ultraviolet arrives from the sun; the surface emits infrared.
Gamma rays play no role in the greenhouse process.
Radio waves are not part of this heat exchange.

check.stem: Which gases absorb the re-emitted heat?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour — the greenhouse gases
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The bulk atmosphere does not trap this heat; greenhouse gases do.
Argon absorbs essentially none of it.
Ground ozone is not the named trapping gas set.

check.stem: What fraction of the re-emitted heat escapes to space?

options.text: Some escapes, while the rest is trapped by greenhouse gases
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
If all escaped, the Earth would freeze.
Part of the heat does reflect back into space.
All surface heat behaves the same way.

check.stem: Why is the greenhouse effect described as essential?

options.text: Because it keeps the planet warm enough for life to survive
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Rainfall depends on the water cycle, not directly on this trapping.
Sunlight passes through; heat is what gets trapped.
Light powers photosynthesis, not trapped heat.

check.stem: Put the greenhouse sequence in the correct order.

options.text: Solar radiation enters, the surface absorbs and re-emits heat, gases trap part of it
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Gases trap sunlight before it lands
options.explanation: Gases trap outgoing heat, not incoming light.
Absorption happens first, then re-emission.

options.text: Heat leaves before it is trapped
options.explanation: Trapping follows re-emission.

check.stem: State what the greenhouse effect is.
check.modelAnswer: The greenhouse effect is the natural trapping of heat in the atmosphere of the Earth by greenhouse gases.

check.stem: Name three greenhouse gases that trap heat in the atmosphere.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are greenhouse gases that absorb and trap heat.

check.stem: Explain why the planet would freeze without greenhouse gases.
check.modelAnswer: Without greenhouse gases, re-emitted heat would escape to space unchecked, so the surface would lose warmth and drop below the level that supports life.

check.stem: On a cloudless desert night, temperature drops sharply. Link to the mechanism.
check.modelAnswer: Dry, cloudless air holds little water vapour, so less re-emitted heat is trapped and the desert surface cools quickly overnight.

lessons.title: Turning Up the Thermostat
sourceHeadings: The consequences of an enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming
lessons.opening: Human activities raise greenhouse gas levels, so more heat is trapped than nature intends: the average temperature of the Earth climbs above normal, and the resulting global warming reshapes oceans, weather, habitats and species distributions.
keyPoints: The enhanced greenhouse effect arises when human activities raise greenhouse gas levels.
Burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture all add to the trapped heat.
The average temperature of the Earth rises above normal, causing global warming and climate change.
Consequences include melting ice caps, rising seas, extreme weather, habitat loss, falling biodiversity and spreading pests and disease.

low.restatement: More gas means more trapped heat, and the extra warmth reshapes oceans, weather and wildlife.
low.analogy: Turning a thermostat up in every room of the planet at once, with ice melting in the freezer.
low.examPointer: Group the consequences: oceans, extreme weather, habitats, biodiversity, migration and disease.

medium.restatement: The enhancement is anthropogenic — fossil fuel combustion, deforestation and agriculture push gas levels up — and the trapped extra heat raises the average temperature, melting polar ice, lifting seas, intensifying storms, degrading habitats, cutting biodiversity and driving pests and disease into new regions.
medium.analogy: A city whose heating is left running while its cool rooms (the forests) are stripped out, so every system overheats together.
medium.examPointer: For consequence questions, list at least three distinct effects rather than rewording one.

check.stem: What turns a natural greenhouse effect into an enhanced one?

options.text: Human activities raising the levels of greenhouse gases
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Volcanic activity cools the planet; enhancement comes from gases.
Solar weakening would cool, not warm, the surface.
Enhancement means more trapping, not less.

check.stem: Which human activities add greenhouse gases to the atmosphere?

options.text: Burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Trees absorb carbon dioxide; they do not add it.
Recycling reduces emissions; it does not raise them.
Wind generation displaces fossil burning.

options.text: The average temperature of the Earth rising above its normal level
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The term tracks the average, not single days.
The poles are warming fastest, not cooling.
The term is global, not about glasshouses.

check.stem: Which chain of ocean consequences follows warming?

options.text: Warmer oceans melt polar ice, raising sea levels and causing flooding and coral bleaching
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Warming, not cooling, drives the named effects.
Sea levels rise with meltwater in the account.
Size changes are not the documented consequence.

check.stem: Why does biodiversity fall as warming proceeds?

options.text: Because disrupted food chains and rising extinction rates remove species
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Resilience falls; the account points to disruption and extinction.

options.text: Because all species move to cities
options.explanation: Species migrate to new habitats, not cities.

options.text: Because biodiversity is fixed by latitude
options.explanation: It shifts with habitat loss and disruption.

check.stem: State what causes the enhanced greenhouse effect.
check.modelAnswer: The enhanced greenhouse effect is caused by increasing levels of greenhouse gases released through human activities.

check.stem: Name two consequences of global warming for the oceans.
check.modelAnswer: Ocean temperatures increase, melting polar ice caps and raising sea levels, and warmer water stresses corals, causing bleaching.

check.stem: Explain why deforestation feeds the enhanced greenhouse effect.
check.modelAnswer: Deforestation removes trees that absorbed carbon dioxide, so less carbon is locked away while the cleared material often releases more when burned.

check.stem: A coastal village floods more often than a decade ago. Give the warming link.
check.modelAnswer: Warming raises ocean temperatures and melts polar ice, so sea levels climb and low-lying coastal villages flood more frequently.

glossary.definition: The natural process in which greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere of the Earth.
The heat radiation that the surface of the Earth emits after absorbing sunlight.
The rise of the average temperature of the Earth above its normal level.
The range and variety of different species of organisms on Earth or within an ecosystem.
